candidate.answerReason: The 3×5 board has 15 squares, an odd number, whereas every domino covers two squares. Each other displayed rectangle can be covered by pairing adjacent squares along an even dimension.

methods.label: Count squares in pairs
methods.explanation:
Each domino covers exactly two small squares, so a board covered completely by whole dominoes must contain an even number of squares. The \(3\times5\) board contains
\[
3\cdot5=15
\]
squares. Since \(15\) is odd, pairing its squares always leaves one square uncovered.

We must also check that the other boards can be covered. For the \(3\times4\) and \(4\times4\) boards, pair consecutive squares across each row of four. For the \(4\times5\) board, pair the first row with the second and the third with the fourth, using vertical dominoes. For the \(6\times3\) board, pair rows \(1\) and \(2\), rows \(3\) and \(4\), and rows \(5\) and \(6\). These arrangements cover every square exactly once.

Thus the only board that cannot be covered is the \(\boxed{3\times5}\) board, choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
methods.levelReason: The argument uses elementary multiplication, odd and even numbers, and explicit pairings of neighboring squares.
